primary.description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline page describes a purported New York Times article about Jeffrey Epstein as flattering and says publicist Howard Rubenstein arranged the interview. The page’s title assigns the item a January 3, 2008 date, and its text says Rubenstein’s client list also included the Trump and Kushner families, Rupert Murdoch, and Adnan Khashoggi. These are claims made by the supplied TrumpFile page, not independently established facts about the article or its preparation. The extracted page provides no link to the New York Times story or to evidence for the arrangement; it says source links would be added later. A client relationship, even if accurate, does not show that Trump or Kushner requested, shaped, or approved the coverage. The underlying article’s publication date, text, tone, and Rubenstein’s role remain unconfirmed. This internal draft preserves the page’s specific claim while identifying its limits. It removes the unrelated national-security and war tags and does not state that Trump influenced the article. Keep the entry publication-ineligible until the original article and claim-level documentation can be reviewed.

frozen_original.title: Trump Organization Double-Billed Expenses Through Internal Loans — NY Fraud Trial Finding
frozen_original.synopsis: During New York's civil fraud trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Trump Organization executives engaged in a scheme of double-billing expenses by routing them through internal intercompany loans that were never repaid. The practice artificially inflated the profitability of certain properties while hiding expenses that would reduce asset valuations. The double-billing scheme was systematic enough that Judge Arthur Engoron found it to be a deliberate pattern rather than accounting error. The findings revealed a corporate culture of deliberate financial manipulation stretching back years across multiple Trump business units. Several Trump Organization executives had previously pleaded guilty to related charges.

frozen_original.title: DOGE Fires 1,500 NIH Scientists and Researchers
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency directed the firing of approximately 1,500 NIH scientists, researchers, and support staff — roughly one-sixth of the agency's total workforce — through a combination of mass terminations and buyout programs that stripped the NIH of experienced researchers in cancer, Alzheimer's, HIV, rare diseases, and emerging infectious diseases. Many of those fired were mid-career scientists with unique expertise and active research programs with no clear successors. Ongoing clinical trials enrolling thousands of patients faced disruption or cancellation. NIH grant peer review panels lost quorum as members resigned in protest. Academic medical centers that relied on NIH training grants reported being unable to maintain research programs. Former NIH directors called the firings an act of scientific self-sabotage that would set U.S. biomedical research back a generation.

primary.title: Trump Administration Begins Mass Layoffs Across Health Agencies, Including NIH
primary.description_short: Reuters reported that a 10,000-person reduction began April 1 across U.S. health agencies, including NIH; the 1,500-scientist NIH-only claim is unsupported.
primary.description_medium: Reuters reported that the Trump administration began mass layoffs across U.S. health agencies on April 1, 2025, with NIH among the affected agencies. Its report described about 10,000 staffers across the agencies overall; it did not assign that figure to NIH, identify 1,500 scientists, or establish a one-sixth NIH workforce reduction. This proposed correction retains the NIH-linked layoff event while removing those unsupported specifics.
primary.description_long: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs at U.S. health agencies, Reuters reported, citing multiple sources familiar with the cuts. The report said the layoffs affected roughly 10,000 staffers across several Department of Health and Human Services agencies, including the National Institutes of Health, the FDA, and the CDC. It described some employees receiving dismissal notices and being barred from entering their workplaces. Reuters did not say that NIH alone lost 1,500 scientists or researchers, did not report that the reduction equaled one-sixth of NIH’s workforce, and did not verify the frozen synopsis’s claims about particular specialties, trials, peer-review panels, or training programs. This corrected card keeps the sourced health-agency layoffs that included NIH, gives the date and figure at the agency-wide scope supported by reporting, and drops the unsupported NIH-only details. The reported layoffs were actual notices and dismissals, but later workforce totals, reversals, and lasting research consequences are outside this source and remain unassessed.
primary.date_basis: Reuters dates the reported mass-layoff start to Tuesday, April 1, 2025.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Administration Begins Mass Layoffs Across Health Agencies, Including NIH
corrected_proposal.description_short: Reuters reported that a 10,000-person reduction began April 1 across U.S. health agencies, including NIH; the 1,500-scientist NIH-only claim is unsupported.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Reuters reported that the Trump administration began mass layoffs across U.S. health agencies on April 1, 2025, with NIH among the affected agencies. Its report described about 10,000 staffers across the agencies overall; it did not assign that figure to NIH, identify 1,500 scientists, or establish a one-sixth NIH workforce reduction. This proposed correction retains the NIH-linked layoff event while removing those unsupported specifics.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs at U.S. health agencies, Reuters reported, citing multiple sources familiar with the cuts. The report said the layoffs affected roughly 10,000 staffers across several Department of Health and Human Services agencies, including the National Institutes of Health, the FDA, and the CDC. It described some employees receiving dismissal notices and being barred from entering their workplaces. Reuters did not say that NIH alone lost 1,500 scientists or researchers, did not report that the reduction equaled one-sixth of NIH’s workforce, and did not verify the frozen synopsis’s claims about particular specialties, trials, peer-review panels, or training programs. This corrected card keeps the sourced health-agency layoffs that included NIH, gives the date and figure at the agency-wide scope supported by reporting, and drops the unsupported NIH-only details. The reported layoffs were actual notices and dismissals, but later workforce totals, reversals, and lasting research consequences are outside this source and remain unassessed.
corrected_proposal.date_basis: Reuters dates the reported mass-layoff start to Tuesday, April 1, 2025.
